newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn coalition wants to let Soviet deserters stay.
newsitem.headline: Bonn coalition wants to let Soviet deserters stay.

text.p: Germany's ruling coalition parties agreed in principle on Tuesday that about 600 deserters from the former Soviet Army in East Germany should not be deported but allowed to stay.

Most of the soldiers have had asylum applications turned down even though they say they will face trial and lengthy prison sentences if they are sent home to Russia or Ukraine. Many faced imminent deportation.
Government sources said the coalition parties had decided at a meeting on Tuesday to recommend to the 16 federal states that the men and their families should be given conditional residence rights.

The men, who defected in the period after German unification in 1990, are all that is left of a Soviet garrison in communist East Germany which once numbered 340,000, and which was taken over by Russia when the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991.

Interior Minister Manfred Kanther is due to present a report on the matter to parliament's interior affairs committee on Wednesday. Any formal decision would have to be taken by the assembled interior ministers of the states.
The opposition Greens, who have taken up the deserters' cause, welcomed Tuesday's move.
"This will close the last chapter of the superpower confrontation with a humane epilogue," said Greens legal affairs spokesman Volker Beck.

The soldiers say Western intelligence officers interrogated them at the Federal Office for Asylum Applications in Nuremberg, when they were applying for political asylum, and told them it would improve their chances of success.
Although it is unlikely that all were able to provide much valuable information to Western intelligence, they say any such contact would be seen as treason at home.
Russian law prescribes a sentence of up to 10 years for desertion and up to 20 years for treason.
But for the German government, desertion alone is not a reason for political asylum to be given, nor is mere contact with Western intelligence services.
Bonn said in a statement last month that 63 deserters and 55 family members had been given asylum, and 1,025 applications had been rejected.
